project's Java style rules or its commit conventions, so both were being

Add two project skills, each a condensed, actionable checklist sourced
from the official SE-EDU guides:
- seedu-java-coding-standard, from
  https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/java/intermediate.html
- seedu-git-standard, from
  https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/git.html

so the source of truth for each standard lives in one place.

Rename yapBot -> YapBot and yapBotException -> YapBotException, and update

README's setup instructions. The product's own branding ("yapBot" the
chatbot, "yapBot.txt"/"yapBot.jar" file names) is left as-is, since only
the Java identifiers were in violation, not the product name.

An audit against the rest of the standard (naming, layout, statements,
imports) found no other violations.

commitResults.messageTitle: seedu-git-standard: Add a line-length verification step
commitResults.messageBody:

in commit 827d9cd that ran 73 and 74 characters, over the 72-char wrap
limit. The rule itself was correct; the gap was that the skill never
told whoever applies it to actually measure line lengths, so it relied
on eyeballing prose while writing, which is unreliable.

Add a Verification section with a concrete check (awk over the drafted
subject/body) to run before committing, and a reminder that fixing a
violation after committing means rewriting an already-pushed commit.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-9: Find tasks by keyword
commitResults.messageBody:
Add a "find <keyword>" command that lists tasks whose description
contains the given keyword, without modifying the task list.

- TaskList.findMatching(keyword) filters and returns an exactly-sized
  array of matches, so callers don't need a separate count like
  toArray()/size() do.
- FindCommand extracts and validates the keyword at execute() time,
  matching how mark/unmark/delete defer their own argument validation
  rather than doing it in the Parser.
- Ui.showMatchingTasks() prints results with the same numbered format
  as showTaskList(), under a distinct "matching tasks" header.
- Parser routes "find" to FindCommand, and the unrecognized-command
  hint messages now mention it alongside the other commands.

Matching is a case-sensitive substring check, the simplest
interpretation that satisfies the spec's example.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-10: Add JavaFX GUI
commitResults.messageBody:
YapBot has been console-only through Level-9. This adds the JavaFX
GUI increment: a window with a text field and a scrolling
conversation view, replacing stdin/stdout as the default way to
interact with the bot (./gradlew run and the shadow jar now launch
it by default), while keeping the console entry point (yapbot.YapBot)
intact and unaffected.

The GUI reuses Parser/Command/TaskList/Storage exactly as the console
loop does; only the input/output layer differs. To avoid duplicating
every message string, Ui gained a single protected output(String)
hook that the console Ui still routes to System.out.println, and a
new GuiUi subclass overrides it to buffer text instead, so both front
ends share one definition of what each message says.

New yapbot.gui package: YapBotGui (drives one GUI session and returns
response text instead of printing it), Main/Launcher (JavaFX
application entry point; Launcher exists so the shadow jar doesn't
hit the "missing JavaFX runtime components" error), MainWindow
(FXML controller), and DialogBox (one conversation row).

Testing: YapBotGuiTest covers the GUI's response logic directly (no
JavaFX toolkit needed). MainWindowTestFX drives the real window via
TestFX and verifies it end-to-end, but needs a focused interactive
desktop to run reliably - Monocle's headless mode does not work on
Windows (the JavaFX thread never starts under it), so this test is
split into its own guiTest Gradle task instead of running as part of
the default test task, keeping `./gradlew test` reliable everywhere.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-10: Stabilize guiTest against first-window focus race
commitResults.messageBody:
guiTest was failing on whichever test method JUnit happened to run
first in the class, regardless of what command it typed - confirmed
by temporarily forcing "bye" to run first, which failed the same way
"todo" had. The window's very first show() doesn't always finish
being focused by the OS before TestFX's robot starts sending clicks
and keystrokes to it, so the first test's input can land before the
window is ready to receive it.

Add a short sleep before each test's interactions to give window
activation time to complete, and correct a docstring that still
mentioned Monocle after headless testing was dropped as unworkable
on Windows.

commitResults.messageTitle: Assert index and capacity invariants in TaskList
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList.get/delete/markAsDone/markAsNotDone accept a raw index
with no bounds checking of their own; they rely entirely on the
caller having already gone through validateIndex(). That reliance
was implicit and undocumented, so a future caller could pass a bad
index and get a confusing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of
a clear signal that the caller itself is at fault.

Add assertions stating this precondition explicitly at each of
those methods, plus at add() (size must be below capacity once the
isFull() guard has passed) and the loaded-array constructor
(loadedCount must fit within MAX_CAPACITY, since Storage.load()
already enforces that on its side).

These are programmer errors, not bad user input, so assert is the
right tool here: it documents the assumption for readers and fails
loudly in development/testing, while costing nothing in a normal
run, where assertions are disabled by default.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_015fYUSC9G6zWQesKdxvoAnT

commitResults.messageTitle: Assert non-null/non-blank fields at task boundaries
commitResults.messageBody:
Task, Deadline and Event take a description (and by/from/to) on
faith: nothing in these constructors checks that the fields are
non-null or non-blank. That's fine as long as every caller already
validated them, but the constructors themselves gave no hint that
this was an assumption rather than an oversight.

Both real callers already do validate: Parser rejects empty/blank
fields before building a task, and Storage rejects blank fields
while parsing a save-file line. Assert the same conditions in the
constructors so the assumption is visible right where it is relied
upon, and so a future third caller that skips validation fails
fast with a clear message instead of silently storing bad data.

Also assert non-null in Parser.parse() (Ui.readCommand() throws
rather than ever returning null) and in TaskList.findMatching()
(FindCommand already validates the keyword before calling it), for
the same reason: both are internal preconditions enforced by a
single caller today, not user-facing input to validate with an
exception.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_015fYUSC9G6zWQesKdxvoAnT

commitResults.messageTitle: build.gradle: Enable assertions for `./gradlew run`
commitResults.messageBody:
The JVM ignores assert statements unless it is started with -ea;
without it, the assumptions just documented in TaskList, Parser
and the Task hierarchy would never actually be checked when running
the app normally, only under the test task (whose enableAssertions
defaults to true in Gradle).

Set applicationDefaultJvmArgs = ['-ea'] so both `./gradlew run` and
the generated start scripts pick it up automatically. This does not
cover the packaged, standalone yapBot.jar: a user launching that
directly with `java -jar` still needs to pass -ea themselves, since
a jar's manifest cannot set JVM flags for its own launch.

commitResults.messageBody: Use assertions to document code invariants

commitResults.messageTitle: Storage: Extract per-type builders out of buildTask
commitResults.messageBody:
buildTask() was 34 lines long, over the guideline's 30-line limit,
because it interleaved three unrelated concerns in one switch: the
todo case's field-count check, the deadline case's field-count and
date-parsing logic, and the event case's field-count and blank-field
checks. Reading it meant tracking three different levels of detail
at once (dispatch vs. per-type validation), which is exactly the
single-level-of-abstraction principle this violates.

Extract buildTodo/buildDeadline/buildEvent, one per case, each
handling only its own type's validation. buildTask itself is now a
short, uniform dispatcher: pick the type, delegate, or reject an
unknown one. No behavior changes; same exceptions, same messages.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_015fYUSC9G6zWQesKdxvoAnT

commitResults.messageTitle: Replace command-keyword-length magic numbers with constants
commitResults.messageBody:
Parser.parseTodo/parseDeadline/parseEvent and FindCommand's
extractKeyword each sliced the command text with a raw literal
(substring(4), substring(8), substring(5)) that silently meant
"the length of 'todo'/'deadline'/'event'/'find'". Nothing in the
code said so; a reader has to count characters in a string literal
elsewhere in the file to see why that particular number appears,
and the number would silently go stale if that keyword's spelling
ever changed.

Introduce named COMMAND_WORD_* constants for each keyword and
derive every slice length from `.length()` on the constant instead.
This also removes the implicit duplication between the keyword
literal used for dispatch (in Parser.parse) and its length used for
slicing (in the corresponding parse method): now there is exactly
one place each keyword is spelled out.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_015fYUSC9G6zWQesKdxvoAnT

commitResults.messageTitle: Deduplicate the task-list max-capacity magic number
commitResults.messageBody:
The "100" that bounds a TaskList's size existed in three unrelated
places: TaskList.MAX_CAPACITY (the real limit TaskList enforces),
YapBotGui.MAX_TASKS (a separately-named constant with the same
value, sized purely to match), and a bare literal 100 in YapBot.main
sizing the array it hands to Storage.load. Three copies of the same
fact, one of them not even named, is a magic number and a
duplication problem at once: nothing enforces that they stay equal,
and changing TaskList's real capacity would silently desync the
other two, letting Storage.load fill an array TaskList can't fully
accept.

Make TaskList.MAX_CAPACITY public, document it as the capacity's
single source of truth, and have YapBot, YapBotGui and the test
that previously kept its own private copy all reference it directly
instead of re-declaring the value.

commitResults.messageBody: Improve code quality

commitResults.messageTitle: TaskList: Use a stream to implement findMatching
commitResults.messageBody:
findMatching built its result by hand: allocate a same-size scratch
array, walk the tasks with an index, append a match and bump a
separate matchCount, then copy down to the real size at the end.
That machinery exists only to express "keep the tasks whose
description contains keyword", which is a plain filter.

Replace it with Arrays.stream(tasks, 0, size).filter(...).toArray(),
which says exactly that and drops the scratch array, the manual
count, and the trailing copyOf. Same behavior: an empty array when
nothing matches, matches kept in original list order.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_015fYUSC9G6zWQesKdxvoAnT

commitResults.messageTitle: Storage: Use a stream to implement buildFileContent
commitResults.messageBody:
buildFileContent walked the array with an index and appended each
task's toFileFormat() plus a line separator onto a shared
StringBuilder. That's a plain map (task -> its file-format line
with a trailing separator) followed by a join.

Replace it with Arrays.stream(tasks, 0, taskCount).map(...).collect
(Collectors.joining()). Appending the separator inside the map step,
then joining with an empty delimiter, keeps the exact same output as
before, including a trailing separator after the last task and an
empty string when taskCount is 0 (StorageTest's save-file assertions
pass unchanged).

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the Priority enum
commitResults.messageBody:
Adding the C-Priority extension: tasks can be tagged high/medium/low
priority. Start with the vocabulary itself, independent of where it
plugs into Task/Storage/Parser: a Priority enum with a fromInput()
factory that matches a level's name case-insensitively and rejects
anything else with a clear message, the same shape as how
Parser.parseDeadlineDate wraps LocalDate.parse.

Levels are a fixed enum rather than free text or a numeric scale,
per spec: exactly HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW, no shorthand. Enum's own
toString() already yields "HIGH"/"MEDIUM"/"LOW", which doubles as
both the display word and the save-file word once this gets wired
in — no separate formatting method needed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add priority display and storage to the Task hierarchy
commitResults.messageBody:
Wire Priority into Task and its three subclasses: a priority field
defaulting to null (no priority, per spec), a getter/setter, and
display/storage support.

Display: Task.toString() now inserts "[LEVEL]" right after the
status icon, before the description, only when a priority is set;
with none set, output is byte-for-byte identical to before this
change (existing TaskTest/TodoTest/DeadlineTest/EventTest cases all
still pass unmodified). Todo/Deadline/Event's own "[T]"/"[D]"/"[E]"
prefixing and (by:.../from:...to:...) suffixing are untouched, since
they just wrap Task.toString().

Storage: priority must always be the line's *last* field, after any
type-specific fields, so old save files without it stay
distinguishable by field count alone once Storage is updated to
accept it (next commit). Task gains a protected appendPriorityField
helper that appends " | " + priority (or nothing, if unset); each
subclass's toFileFormat() calls it last, after its own fields, since
Todo has none of its own and previously relied entirely on
inheritance, it needs a new override just to make that call.

commitResults.messageTitle: Storage: Load an optional trailing priority field
commitResults.messageBody:
Each buildTodo/buildDeadline/buildEvent required an exact field
count, so a save file with the new trailing priority field appended
would fail every line's field-count check and get skipped as
corrupted -- even though the file itself is perfectly valid under
the new format.

Widen each check from "exactly N" to "N or N+1"; when it's N+1,
parse the extra trailing field as a priority via the new shared
applyOptionalPriority helper and apply it to the already-built task.
The by/from/to reads at parts[3]/parts[4] are untouched, since
priority is always the *last* field regardless of type -- this is
what keeps old-format lines (no priority) and new-format lines
(with one) unambiguous by field count alone, and needs no version
marker or migration step.

An invalid trailing value throws the same way other bad fields do,
so a corrupted priority is skipped with a warning by the existing
tryLoadLine handling, not a crash.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_015fYUSC9G6zWQesKdxvoAnT

commitResults.messageTitle: Parser: Support an optional /priority flag on add commands
commitResults.messageBody:
Wire the creation-time half of the syntax: todo/deadline/event can
now end with "/priority <level>" (per spec, always the last flag on
the line).

Add one extractPriority() helper, called first in each of
parseTodo/parseDeadline/parseEvent, right after the command's
keyword is stripped -- before any /by or /from/to splitting. It
returns the text with the flag removed (a no-op if there was none)
paired with the parsed Priority (or null), via a small private
TextWithPriority record. Because extraction happens before the
existing split logic runs, that logic is completely untouched: it
already only ever sees a priority-free remainder.

An invalid or missing level after /priority throws immediately, the
same way a bad deadline date does, so no task is added.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_015fYUSC9G6zWQesKdxvoAnT

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the 'priority' command to change a task's priority
commitResults.messageBody:
The /priority flag only covers setting a priority at creation time;
per spec there also needs to be a way to change (or first set) an
existing task's priority afterward, mirroring mark/unmark.

Add PriorityCommand, dispatched from a new "priority" branch in
Parser.parse(). It parses "priority <index> <level>" itself (split
on the first whitespace) rather than reusing TaskList.validateIndex
end-to-end, since that method assumes its whole post-keyword
argument is the index alone. It does reuse validateIndex for the
actual number/range checks, by re-assembling "priority <index>" as
the sub-string passed in -- that keeps the well-tested shared method
untouched. The one case it special-cases is an empty list: reusing
validateIndex there would print "...nothing to priority.", which
doesn't read as a sentence the way "...nothing to mark." does, so
this checks that first and reports "...nothing to change the
priority of." instead.

Ui gains showPriorityChanged(Task), same shape as showTaskMarked.

commitResults.messageTitle: docs: Document setting a task's priority
commitResults.messageBody:
docs/README.md is a placeholder template ("## Feature ABC" / "##
Feature XYZ" slots meant to be filled in as real features are
documented); nothing had replaced either slot yet. Replace "Feature
ABC" with real content for this increment: the /priority flag at
creation, the priority change command, and what happens when neither
